The majority of reciters read ﴿"hudan wa rahmatan"﴾ in the accusative as a circumstantial accusative (hal) from the indefinite "tilka"; it cannot be from "al-Kitab," because that is a genitive construct (mudaf ilayhi). Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read it in the nominative, with the implied meaning "it is guidance." He specified it for the doers of good in that they benefit from it, and they have looked at it with the eye of reality; otherwise it is guidance in itself. In the reading of Ibn Mas'ud: "hudan wa bushra lil-mu'minin" (guidance and good news for the believers).

Then the Exalted described the doers of good as those who have certainty regarding the resurrection and everything the Messenger ﷺ brought, and who establish prayer and give zakah. Among their characteristics is what the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said when Jibril (peace be upon him) asked him about excellence (ihsan): "That you worship Allah as if you see Him, and if you do not see Him, then indeed He sees you." The hadith continues.

(p-41) And His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And among the people is one who purchases idle talk﴾. It is narrated that it was revealed concerning a Qurashi man who bought a singing slave-girl who would sing satirizing and reviling the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, so the verse was revealed concerning that. It is narrated from Abu Umamah al-Bahili that the Prophet ﷺ said: "Buying singing slave-girls and selling them is forbidden," and he recited this verse, and said: "In this regard this verse was revealed to me." Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn 'Abbas, Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah, and Mujahid explained it in this way. Al-Hasan said: idle talk is musical instruments and singing.

Some people said: it was revealed concerning al-Nadr ibn al-Harith, because he bought the books of Rustam and Isfandiyar, and he would take the place of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and relate those falsehoods to them, saying: "I am better at storytelling than Muhammad." Qatadah said: the purchase in this verse is figurative, and it was revealed only concerning the talk of Quraysh, their diversion with the affair of Islam, and their immersion in falsehoods.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

Leaving what must be done and adopting these forbidden things is, as it were, a purchase of them, in line with His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Those are the ones who purchased error in exchange for guidance﴾ [al-Baqarah: 16]. Mutarrif said: buying idle talk is preferring it. Qatadah said: perhaps he does not spend money on it, but listening to it is his purchase. al-Dahhak said: idle talk is shirk. Mujahid also said: idle talk is the drum, and this is a kind of singing.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

What is more likely is that the verse was revealed concerning idle talk that is attached to disbelief, which is why the wording of the verse is so severe, with His saying: ﴿to mislead from the way of Allah without knowledge and take it in ridicule﴾ and the threat of a humiliating punishment. As for the word "purchase," it admits of both literal and figurative meaning, as we have explained. "Idle talk" is everything that diverts, such as singing, obscenity, and the like. The meaning of the verse remains in the community of Muhammad ﷺ, but not so that they go astray from the way of Allah through disbelief, nor so that they take the signs in ridicule, nor is this threat upon them; rather, it is so that it wastes worship, cuts them off for a time from what is disliked, and because they are among the sinners. Deficient souls seek to complete that deficiency through talk. They have made talk a kind of entertainment. It was said to one of them: "Do you get bored of talk?" He said: "Only the old, the repeated, becomes tiresome, for a new talk has a freshness that prevents boredom."

Nafi', 'Asim, and al-Hasan read ﴿"liyudilla"﴾ with a damma on the yā'. Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr read it with a fatha. In the codex of Ubayy: "liyudilla al-nasa 'an sabili Allah." Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, and Hafs from 'Asim read ﴿"wa yattakhidha"﴾ in the accusative, coordinated with "liyudilla." The rest read ﴿"wa yattakhidha"﴾ in the nominative, coordinated with ﴿"yashtari."﴾

The pronoun in "wa yattakhidha" may refer to "al-Kitab al-Hakim" mentioned first, it may refer to "the way," and it may refer to "the talks," since "hadith" is a collective noun with the sense of "ahadith." Likewise "sabil Allah" is a collective noun, and each interpretation of "hadith" has a corresponding interpretation of "the way" that fits it.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 31, verses 7–11:

The Exalted's saying:

﴿And when Our verses are recited to him, he turns away arrogantly, as if he had not heard them, as if there were deafness in his ears. So give him tidings of a painful punishment.﴾ ﴿Indeed, those who believe and do righteous deeds will have gardens of bliss,﴾ ﴿abiding therein forever. The promise of Allah is true, and He is the Mighty, the Wise.﴾ ﴿He created the heavens without pillars that you can see, and He cast into the earth firm mountains lest it shake with you, and He dispersed therein every kind of moving creature. And We sent down water from the sky and caused to grow therein every noble kind of plant.﴾ ﴿This is the creation of Allah. So show Me what those other than Him have created. Rather, the wrongdoers are in manifest error.﴾

This is evidence of the disbelief of the one about whom the preceding verse was revealed. Al-"waqr" (deafness) in the ear is the heaviness that makes the perception of what is heard difficult. The tidings of punishment came in a restricted and explicit form, as it was specified and stated explicitly.

When the Exalted mentioned the condition of these disbelievers and threatened them with the Fire for their deeds, He followed it with mention of the believers and what He promised them of the gardens of bliss, so that the difference would be made clear. "Waʿda Allāh" (the promise of Allah) is in the accusative as an infinitive (ḥāl/maṣdar), and "ḥaqqan" (truly) is an emphatic infinitive.

As for the Exalted's saying: ﴿without pillars that you can see﴾ — the pronoun may refer to "the heavens," so the meaning is: the heavens are without pillars, and they are seen as such. This is the saying of al-Ḥasan and others, and "tarawnahā" — on this view — is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl). It is also possible that the pronoun refers to "the pillars" (ʿamad), so that "tarawnahā" is an attributive clause describing the pillars in the genitive position, and the meaning is: the heavens have pillars, but they are not visible. This was said by Mujāhid, and Ibn ʿAbbās (may Allah be pleased with them both) inclined toward it. The first meaning is more correct, and the majority hold it. It is also permissible that "tarawnahā" be in the nominative position as a resumption (qaṭʿ), and then there are no pillars there.

Al-"rawāsī" (firm mountains) are the mountains that are fixed in the earth. The Exalted's saying ﴿lest it shake﴾ means: "lest it not shake." Al-"mayd" is movement to the right and left and what is near that. The Exalted's saying ﴿of every kind (zawj)﴾ means: of every type. In the language, "zawj" means type and category, and it is not the one that is the opposite of "fard" (single). The Exalted's saying ﴿noble (karīm)﴾ may mean praise for the perfection of its craftsmanship and the manifestation of the goodness of its rank and the ordering of the creation within it, in which case it encompasses all kinds, since this meaning is in all of them. It may also mean praise for the nobility of its substance and the goodliness of its appearance, and what souls judge to be superior to others, so as to deserve the title of nobility; in this case the "kinds" are specified in the choicest and most admired things. Since the greatness of the existents is of this nature, He specified the proof with them.

His saying "we caused to grow" encompasses the kinds of animals, the kinds of plants, and minerals.

Then the Exalted confronted the disbelievers, by way of rebuke and the manifestation of proof, with the fact that these things are the creatures of Allah, Blessed and Exalted. Then He asked them to bring forth what the idols and images and others worshipped besides Him have created; that is, they will never create anything. Rather, what Quraysh are in is manifest error. Then He reminded them of the attribute that includes, along with them, others from the nations who did as they did. His saying "mādhā" (what) may be an interrogative "mā" in the nominative position as a subject, with "dhā" as its predicate in the sense of "alladhī" (what/that which), and the returning pronoun omitted. It may also be that "mā" is the object of "arūnī" and "dhā" is a relative element, with "mā" in the sense of "alladhī," and the returning pronoun omitted; the estimated form in both cases is: "khalaqahu" (created it).

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 31, verses 12–13:

The words of the Exalted:

﴿And We certainly gave Luqman wisdom, [saying]: Give thanks to God. Whoever gives thanks, gives thanks only for his own soul. And whoever disbelieves, then indeed God is Self-Sufficient, Praiseworthy.﴾ ﴿And when Luqman said to his son, while advising him: "O my son, do not associate anything with God. Indeed, association [shirk] is a tremendous wrong."﴾

Luqman was a wise man through the wisdom of God, the Exalted. It is correctness in beliefs, and understanding (fiqh) in religion and action. Scholars differed over whether, in addition to this, he was a prophet or only a righteous man.

Ikrimah and al-Sha'bi said that he was a prophet. Mujahid and others said that he was only righteous. Ibn 'Umar, may God be pleased with them both, said: "I heard the Prophet (ﷺ) say: 'Luqman was not a prophet, but he was a servant who reflected greatly and had good certainty. He loved God, so God loved him. He bestowed wisdom upon him and gave him the choice to be made a khalifah who judges with truth. Luqman said: O Lord, if You give me the choice, I accept well-being and leave trial. If You insist upon me, then I hear and obey, for indeed You will protect me.'"

He was a judge among the Children of Israel, a black Nubian with cracked feet and thick lips. This was said by Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib, Mujahid, and Ibn 'Abbas. A man who had once tended sheep with him said to him: "What has brought you, O Luqman, to what I see [of your state]?" He replied: "Truthfulness of speech and silence about what does not concern me."

Ibn al-Musayyib said: He was from the blacks of Egypt, from the Nubians. Khalid ibn al-Rabi' said: He was a carpenter. It was also said that he was a tailor, and it was said that he was a shepherd. The sayings of Luqman are many and transmitted. It was said to him: "Which of the people is the worst?" He said: "The one who does not care if people see him doing evil."

The words of the Exalted, ﴿an ushkur﴾ ("that give thanks"): the particle "an" may be in a position of nasb (accusative) by dropping the preposition (harf al-jarr), meaning "bi-an ushkur lillah" ("by giving thanks to God"). It may also be mufassirah (explanatory "an"), meaning: his wisdom revolved around giving thanks to God, the Exalted, and its meanings. All acts of worship and beliefs fall within giving thanks to God, blessed and exalted. Then the Exalted informed that the benefit of the one who gives thanks returns to him, for he is the one who profits from it. God, the Exalted, is free of need for thanks, so the thanks of servants does not benefit Him. He is Praiseworthy in Himself, so the disbelief of disbelievers does not harm Him. "Hamid" (praiseworthy) means mahmud (praised): that is, He deserves that by His attributes and His essence.

His, the Mighty and Majestic, saying:

﴿We have enjoined upon man (concerning) his parents. His mother bore him in weakness upon weakness, and his weaning is in two years: "Be grateful to Me and to your parents; to Me is the final destination."﴾ ﴿But if they strive with you to make you associate with Me that of which you have no knowledge, do not obey them, and keep company with them in this world with kindness, and follow the way of those who turn to Me in repentance. Then to Me is your return, and I will inform you of what you used to do.﴾

These two verses are an interjection (i'tiraḍ) within the admonition of Luqman. al-Tabari held that they are part of the meaning of Luqman's words and among what he intended, but this is not well-founded. The fact that the two verses concern Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas, as he mentions afterwards, weakens the view that they are among what Luqman said. What seems more likely is that it is an interjection during the admonition, and this does not spoil the first part of it or the last part. When he finished these two verses (p-47), he returned to the admonition, with the assumption of an implied "and Luqman also said," then he abbreviated that because the preceding context indicates it.

In this verse, Allah, the Exalted, placed the mother and the father together in the rank of the injunction concerning them, then He singled out the mother with a degree of mention of the carrying (of the child) and a degree of mention of the nursing. Thus the mother has three ranks, and the father has one. Something similar to this is the statement of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), when a man said to him: "Who is most deserving of my good companionship?" He said: "Your mother." He said: "Then who?" He said: "Your mother." He said: "Then who?" He said: "Your mother." He said: "Then who?" He said: "Then your father." So he made the father one quarter of the goodness, like the verse.

﴿Weakness upon weakness﴾ means: weakness upon weakness. It was said: it is an indication of the hardship of the pregnancy and the hardship of the birth after it. It was said: it is an indication of the weakness of the child and the weakness of the mother along with it. It is possible that it indicates the gradual progression of her condition in increasing weakness, so it is as if He did not specify two weaknesses, but rather as if He said: his mother carried him while weakness keeps increasing upon weakness until its term is completed. 'Isa al-Thaqafi read "wahnan 'ala wahnin" with a fatḥah on the hāʾ (wahnan), and it is narrated from Abu 'Amr. Both have one meaning.

The people (the majority of readers) read "wa-fiṣāluhu" (fiṣāluhu), while al-Ḥasan, al-Jaḥdari, and Ya'qub read "wa-faṣluhu" (faṣluhu). By fiṣāl he indicated the defining of the period of nursing, expressing it by its endpoint and its termination. The scholars are unanimous "upon the two years" as the period of nursing with regard to the rulings concerning maintenance and expenses. As for the prohibition of milk (relationship through breastfeeding), one group limited it to the two years, with no addition and no reduction. Another group said: the two years and what is connected to them, such as a month or so, when the suckling is continuous, falls under one ruling of prohibition. Another group said: if the child was weaned before the two years and left off milk, then what he drinks after that within the two years does not create prohibition.

His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿an ushkur (that give thanks)﴾ may be understood as: "bi-an ushkur" (by giving thanks), and it may be (p-48) explanatory (mufassira). His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿to Me is the final destination﴾ is a warning (tawa'ud) within the injunction.

His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿But if they strive with you﴾ — the verse. It is related that these two verses were revealed concerning Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas, and that is because his mother, who was Hamna bint Abi Sufyan ibn Umayya, swore that she would not eat or drink until he abandoned his religion and returned to the religion of his forefathers and his people. Sa'd persisted in Islam. It is related that when thirst overcame her, they would force open her mouth, and it is also related: "they would split her mouth open" (shajjarū), meaning they opened it with a stick or the like and poured in what would keep her alive. The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

The first verse agrees with the goodness toward the two parents and its ruling, then it ruled that this does not apply in disbelief and acts of disobedience. The overall principle of this chapter is that obedience to the parents is not observed in committing a major sin, nor in abandoning an obligation upon every individual (fard 'ayn). Obedience to them is binding in permissible matters, and abandoning acts of worship is disliked in the case of the recommended (al-nadb, that which is recommended but not obligatory). Among this is the matter of communal jihad (jihad al-kifaya, an obligation upon the community as a whole, which is fulfilled if some perform it). Responding to the mother during prayer is (allowed) while it is possible to repeat the prayer. His saying: ﴿and keep company with them in this world with kindness﴾ means: the two parents who are disbelievers, that is: maintain ties with them through wealth, and invite them with gentleness. **Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on Surah Luqman, verses 16–19**

The words of the Exalted:

﴿O my son, indeed if it be the weight of a mustard seed and should be within a rock or in the heavens or in the earth, Allah will bring it forth. Indeed, Allah is Subtle and Acquainted.﴾ ﴿O my son, establish prayer, enjoin what is right, forbid what is wrong, and bear patiently what befalls you. Indeed, that is of the matters requiring determination.﴾ ﴿And do not turn your cheek [in contempt] toward people, and do not walk through the earth exultantly. Indeed, Allah does not like everyone self-deluded and boastful.﴾ ﴿And be moderate in your walking and lower your voice. Indeed, the most disagreeable of voices is the voice of donkeys.﴾

The meaning: Luqman said, "O my son." This statement of Luqman's was intended only to inform his son of the extent of Allah's power, which is as far as he could make him understand. The mustard seed (khardal) is said to have no weight perceptible to the senses, since it does not tip a scale. This verse states that Allah the Exalted has encompassed it with knowledge. The words of Allah, ﴿mithqal habba﴾ ("the weight of a grain"), are an expression that can apply to substances, meaning "the quantity of a grain," and can apply to deeds, meaning what weighs as much as a grain in terms of equivalence. The apparent sense of the verse is that he meant something hidden among things, the size of a grain. This is supported by what is narrated: "that the son of Luqman asked his father about a grain that falls into [the depths of] the sea, does Allah know it? So Luqman answered him with this verse." Many of the exegetes mention that he meant deeds, sins, and acts of obedience. This is supported by the words ﴿Allah will bring it forth﴾, meaning, nothing escapes Him. In this sense, the admonition contains both hope and fear, combined with clarifying the power of Allah the Exalted. In the other view there is neither hope nor fear.

Among what supports the view of those who said "it is of the substances" is the recitation of 'Abd al-Karim al-Jazari: ﴿fatakinn﴾ with a kasra on the kaf and a shaddah on the nun, from *kunn*, which is that which is covered.

The majority of people recited ﴿in takun﴾ with a *ta'* at the beginning, and ﴿mithqal﴾ in the accusative as the predicate (*khabar*) of *kana* (the auxiliary verb), whose subject (*ism*) is an implied pronoun; its estimated reference is: "your question" according to what is narrated, or: "the disobedience" or "the obedience" according to the second view. The pronoun in ﴿innaha﴾ is the pronoun of the matter (*damir al-qissa*). Nafi' alone recited ﴿takunu mithqalu﴾ with a *ta'* and with ﴿mithqalu﴾ in the nominative as the subject of *kana*, which is the complete *kana* (*al-kana al-tamma*), and he attached to the *mithqal* a verb bearing the feminine marker, since it is attached to a feminine noun of which it is a part. This is like the saying of the poet:

They walked as spear-shafts sway, whose tips are swayed
By the gentle passing of the breezes.

This is the recitation of al-A'raj and Abu Ja'far.

As for His words ﴿fi sakhratin﴾ ("within a rock"), it has been said that He meant the rock on which the earth, the fish and the water rest, and which is on the back of an angel. It has also been said: it is a rock in the wind.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

All of this is weak, not established by any chain of transmission. The meaning of the statement is only exaggeration and thoroughness in conveying the point, that is: His power is an example of what exists within the crevices of a rock and what exists in the heavens and on the earth. Qatada recited ﴿fatakinn﴾ with a kasra on the kaf and without shaddah, from *wakana yakinu*, and the recitation of 'Abd al-Karim ﴿fatakinn﴾ has preceded.

As for His words ﴿Allah will bring it forth﴾: if He meant substances, then the meaning is: He will bring it forth if it is needed, or if it was sustenance or the like. If He meant deeds, then its meaning is: He will bring forth its mention and its preservation, in order to recompense for it with reward or punishment. ﴿Subtle and Acquainted﴾ are two attributes suitable for manifesting the wonders of power.

Then he charged his son with the greatest acts of obedience, which are prayer, enjoining what is right, and forbidding what is wrong. This is something he intends only after the son has himself embodied it in his certainty and restrained himself from what is wrong. Here, these are all the acts of obedience and virtues together.

His words ﴿and bear patiently what befalls you﴾ require urging to change the wrong, even if harm reaches you. This indicates that the one who changes wrong is sometimes harmed. This degree is by way of recommendation (*nadb*) and strength in the cause of Allah the Mighty and Majestic; as for obligation, it is not so.

His words ﴿Indeed, that is of the matters requiring determination﴾ mean: among what Allah has determined and commanded. It is also possible that this is among the noble characteristics and the resolutions of people of firmness, and of those who travel the path of salvation. The first is more correct, and a group said both.

Nafi', Abu 'Amr, Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, and Ibn Muhaysin recited ﴿wa la tusa'ir﴾. Ibn Kathir, 'Asim, Ibn 'Amir, al-Hasan, Mujahid, and Abu Ja'far recited ﴿wa la tusa''ir﴾ (with *tashdid*). al-Jahdari recited ﴿wa la tus'ir﴾ with the *sad* sukun, and the meaning is close. *Sa'ar* is inclination, and from it is the saying of the Bedouin: "The age has straightened my turned neck after I had straightened its turning," and from it is the saying of 'Amr ibn Hunayy al-Taghlibi:

We all walk slowly,
We all seek game,
Except 'Amr ibn 'Ubayd.

Loud of appearance, loud of camels.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 31, verses 20–21:

His, the Exalted and Majestic, words:

﴿Have you not seen that God has subjected to you whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth, and has completed His blessings upon you, outward and inward? Yet among the people is one who disputes about God without knowledge, or guidance, or an illuminating Book.﴾ ﴿And when it is said to them, "Follow what God has sent down," they say, "Rather, we follow what we found our fathers upon." Even if Satan were calling them to the punishment of the Blaze?﴾

This is a verse calling attention to the craftsmanship that indicates the Craftsman, for the subjugation of these great things, such as the sun, the moon, the stars, the clouds, the winds, animals and plants, is only by one who subjugates and possesses them. Yahya ibn 'Imara and Ibn 'Abbas read "wa-asbagha" with the sad (ص) in place of the sin (س), because the letters of elevation (huruf al-isti'la') draw the sin from its lowness toward its height, so it turns into a sad; the majority read it with the sin. Nafi', Abu 'Amr, Hafs from 'Asim, al-Hasan, al-A'raj, Abu Ja'far, Ibn Nisah and others read "ni'amahu" as the plural of ni'ma, like sidra and sidar, with the dal vowelled with a fatha. "Al-zahira" (outward) is health, good form, wealth and other things, and "al-batina" (inward) is beliefs of faith and the like, and reason. Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with them both, said: the outward is Islam and good form, and the inward is what is concealed of evil deeds. It is related in a hadith: "It was said: O Messenger of God (ﷺ), we know the outward; what is the inward? He said: Concealing what, if people saw you doing it, they would despise you."

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

Among the inward blessings are breathing, digestion, nutrition, and countless others, and among the outward is the action of the limbs in obedience. Al-Muhasibi said: the outward blessings are the blessings of this world, and the inward are the blessings of the hereafter. Most people read "ni'matan" in the singular. Mujahid said the intended meaning is "There is no god but God," and Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with them both, said it means Islam. The apparent view to me is that it is a noun of genus, like His words, blessed and exalted: ﴿And if you count the blessing of God, you cannot enumerate it﴾ [al-Nahl: 18].

Then He contrasted with it the disbelievers, on account of the corruption of their state, and they are the ones indicated by His words, "And among the people": al-Naqqash said the reference is to al-Nadr ibn al-Harith and his like, for they used to deny God and associate idols in divinity, and that is their disputation. "Without knowledge" means: no one whose word is accepted has informed them, and they have no guidance of heart nor light of insight by which they establish proof, and they do not seek in this a book by the command of God that gives good news that it is revelation; rather, that is mere claim and conjecture from them. When they are called to follow the revelation of God, they return to pure imitation without proof, and so they take the path of the fathers. Then God, the Exalted, stood them (and they are the ones meant by the questioning) before their following the religion of their fathers: would they be in a state of one who is headed to the punishment of the Blaze? It is as if the speaker among them were saying: they follow the religion of their fathers even if their destination is the Blaze. So the interrogative alif entered upon the conjunctive letter, as the coherence of the speech required. So reflect upon it.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 31, verses 22–26:

Allah the Exalted and Majestic says:

﴿And whoever submits his face to Allah while he is a doer of good has grasped the most trustworthy handhold, and to Allah is the outcome of all affairs.﴾ ﴿And whoever disbelieves, let not his disbelief grieve you. To Us is their return, and We will inform them of what they did. Indeed, Allah is Knowing of what is within the breasts.﴾ ﴿We grant them enjoyment for a little, then We will compel them to a severe punishment.﴾ ﴿And if you asked them, "Who created the heavens and the earth?", they would surely say, "Allah." Say, "Praise be to Allah." But most of them do not know.﴾ ﴿To Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth. Indeed, Allah is the Free of need, the Praiseworthy.﴾

When Allah mentioned the state of the disbelievers, He followed it with mention of the state of the believers, so that the difference would become clear and souls would be moved to seek what is best.

The majority of reciters read ﴿"yuslim"﴾ with a sukun on the sin and a light lam. 'Abdullah ibn Muslim and Abu 'Abd al-Rahman read "yusallim" with a fatha on the sin and a shaddah on the lam. Its meaning is: he sincerely devotes himself, directs himself, and surrenders thereby. "Al-wajh" (the face) here is the bodily organ, used figuratively for intention, because one who intends something faces it with his face; so this was borrowed for meanings. "Al-muhsin" (the doer of good) is one who combines speech and action, and he is the one whom the Messenger of Allah ﷺ described when Jibril (peace be upon him) asked him.

"Al-'urwah al-wuthqa" (the most trustworthy handhold) is a metaphor for the saving matter which is not feared to be broken or deficient. The "'urwa" is the place of suspension, so it is as if the believer is attached to the command of Allah, the Blessed and Exalted, and this was likened to the handhold. "Al-umur" (affairs) is the plural of amr, and it is not the opposite of nahy (prohibition). Then Allah the Exalted and Majestic consoled His Prophet (peace be upon him) regarding his distress at the disbelief and aversion of his people, and commanded him not to grieve over that, but rather to proceed with what he was charged with of conveying the message, and all return to Allah the Exalted. One group read ﴿"yuhzinka"﴾ from the quadriliteral form, and another group read ﴿"yahzunka"﴾ from the triliteral form. "Dhat al-sudur" (what is within the breasts) means what is in them, and the intended meaning of that is the beliefs and opinions. From this is their saying, "The wolf is envied for the one in its belly," and from it is the saying of Abu Bakr al-Siddiq (may Allah be pleased with him): "Dhu batn bint Kharija." "Al-mata' al-qalil" (the little enjoyment) is the lifespan in this world, and "al-'adhab al-ghalidh" (the severe punishment) means the one that is harsh and painful.

Then He established the proof against them regarding the idols, by the fact that they acknowledge that Allah the Exalted is the Creator of the creatures, yet they invoke along with Him another god. The meaning is: say, "Praise be to Allah," for the proof has become manifest against you. His saying, the Exalted, ﴿"bal aktharuhum"﴾ (but most of them) is a turning away from an implied premise, its implied meaning being: their claim is not true, and similar to this. His saying ﴿"aktharuhum"﴾ is on its original basis, because among them are those whose conduct was anomalous, such as Zayd ibn 'Amr ibn Nufayl and Waraqa ibn Nawfal. It is also possible that the reference is to those who are prepared to submit. Then He informed, in the manner of a ruling and decisive judgment, that Allah the Mighty and Majestic has dominion over the heavens and the earth and whatever is in them, meaning: the statements of these people have no meaning and no reality. The meaning is: the One who has no need in His existence or His perfection for anything, and no deficiency in any respect. "Al-Hamid" (the Praiseworthy) means the one who is praised, meaning: He is so in His essence and His attributes.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on Surah 31, verses 27–28**

God Most High says:

Others said that the occasion of revelation was that the Quraysh said: "This speech of Muhammad will finish and come to an end," and so it was revealed. Al-Suddi said: the Quraysh said: "How much Muhammad's speech is!" and so it was revealed.

The purpose of the verse is to inform that the words of God Most High are abundant, and that in themselves they are not finite. The matter has been brought closer to human understanding through what is finite, because it is the furthest extent of abundance that humans are accustomed to. The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This is a view that inclines toward the Mu'tazila (a theological school that holds that the Qur'an is created), in that they regard speech as created. May Allah Most High illuminate our hearts with His guidance.

Abu 'Amr alone among the Seven Readers, along with Ibn Abi Ishaq and 'Isa, read "wal-bahra" (والبحرَ) in the accusative, as a conjunction with "ma" (ما), which is the subject of "anna" (أنَّ). The majority of people read "wal-bahru" (والبحرُ) in the nominative, as a beginning (mubtada'), whose predicate is the clause that follows it, because its implied sense is "his condition is such-and-such." Sibawayh (Sibawayh, the foundational grammarian) estimated it this way. Some grammarians said it is a conjunction with "an" (أنْ), because it occupies a nominative position as the subject.

Another group said: "madda" means that a thing supplies another thing of its own kind, while "amadda" means that a thing supplies what is not part of it. So it is as if the seven seas that are imagined are not part of the existing sea. Ja'far ibn Muhammad read "wal-bahru midaduhu" (والبحرُ مِدادُهُ), where "midad" is a verbal noun. Ibn Mas'ud read "wa-bahrun yamudduhu" (وبحرٌ يَمُدُّهُ). Al-Hasan read "ma nafida kalamu Allah" (ما نَفِدَ كلامُ اللهِ).

Then God Most High mentioned the matter of creation and resurrection: that it is, in all its aspects and in a single person, equal, because all of it is "Be, and it is" (كُنْ فَيَكُونُ). This is what Mujahid said. Al-Naqqash related that this verse was revealed concerning Ubayy ibn Khalaf, Abu al-Aswad and his sons, and Munabbih ibn al-Hajjaj, because "they said: 'O Muhammad, we see the child created gradually, and you say that God will restore us all at once.' So the verse was revealed concerning them."

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 31, verse 29–30:

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He:

﴿Do you not see that Allah causes the night to enter into the day and causes the day to enter into the night, and He has subjected the sun and the moon, each running to a specified term, and that Allah is Acquainted with what you do?﴾ ﴿That is because Allah is the Truth, and what they invoke besides Him is falsehood, and because Allah is the Exalted, the Great.﴾

This is an admonition addressed to the Prophet (ﷺ), and what is intended by it is the whole of creation. It is a lesson pointing to the Creator, the Originator, that the night should be [lengthened] gradually and the day likewise: whatever decreases from one of them is added to the other. Then, conversely, it is divided by the wisdom of the Maker of the world, there is no lord besides Him.

"Yūliju" means: causes to enter. "The specified term" (al-ajal al-musammā) is the Resurrection, when this structure will be undone and the sun will be folded up. The majority of the reciters read "bi-mā ta'malūna" with the ta' from above (taʿmalūna), while ʿAbbās, from Abū ʿAmr, read "yaʿmalūna" with the yā'.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿That is because Allah is the Truth﴾. The reference of "dhālika" (that) is to this lesson and what runs in its course. The meaning of ﴿He is the Truth﴾ is: the attribute of divinity belonging to Him is true (ḥaqq). Thus it is good in speech to supply "dhū" (possessor of), and likewise this principle: whenever a verbal noun is predicated of a concrete entity, the supplied form is "dhū kadhā" (possessor of such-and-such). "Ḥaqq" is a verbal noun, and from it is the saying of the poet:

"Indeed, it is only advance and retreat."

And this is common. When you say "such-and-such is true (ḥaqq)," its meaning is: the characterization of such-and-such by such-and-such is true.

His saying: ﴿and that what they invoke besides Him﴾ may mean the idols, with "mā" in the sense of "alladhī" (that which), and the predication of falsehood (al-bāṭil) of them would be in the manner we mentioned regarding "al-ḥaqq." It is also permissible for "mā" to be a verbal (maṣdarīyah) particle, as if he said: and that your invoking gods besides Him is falsehood, i.e., an act that does not lead to the sought goal. The majority read "tadʿūna" with the ta' from above, while "yadʿūna" with the yā' is read by Ibn Wathhāb, al-Aʿmash, the people of Makkah, and it is narrated from Abū ʿAmr. The rest of the verse is clear.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 31, verses 31–32:

His words, mighty and majestic is He:

﴿Have you not seen that the ships sail upon the sea by the favour of Allah, that He may show you of His signs? Indeed in that are signs for every steadfast, grateful person.﴾ ﴿And when a wave covers them like canopies, they call upon Allah, sincerely devoting religion to Him. But when He delivers them to the land, some of them are moderate. And none rejects Our signs except every treacherous ingrate.﴾

The seeing in His words ﴿"Have you not seen"﴾ is seeing with the eye, upon which contemplation and reflection are built. The one addressed is Muhammad (ﷺ), and the intended meaning is all of mankind. "Al-fulk" (the ships) is both a plural and a singular with one form. Musa ibn al-Zubayr read "al-fulk" with a damma on the lam. His words ﴿"Have you not seen"﴾ may mean what the ships carry of food and provisions, so the ba' (bi) is for attachment (ilsaq). It may also mean by the wind and Allah's subjugation of the sea and the like, so the ba' is the ba' of causation (sabab). The majority read "bi-ni'mah" (by a favour), while Ibn Abi 'Abla read "bi-ni'amat" (by favours), with a fatha on the nun and a kasra on the 'ayn.

Allah mentioned, as a quality of the believer, the one who is steadfast (sabbar) and grateful (shakur) in adversity and in ease. Al-Sha'bi said: "Patience is half of faith, and gratitude is its other half, and certainty is the whole of faith."

"Ghashiya" means it covered, or it approached. "Al-zulal" means the clouds. Muhammad ibn al-Hanafiyya read "ka-al-zilal" (like shades). From this is the saying of al-Nabigha describing the sea:

It is accompanied by them, a green one with shades, on whose edges is the splitting of jars.

In this verse Allah described the state of humans who do not take heed with the proper heeding. The purpose of the verse is to make clear a sign which the intellects bear witness to, that the idols and images have no partnership in it and no role.

As for His words ﴿"Some of them are moderate"﴾, al-Hasan said: among them is a believer who knows Allah's right in these favours. Mujahid said: he means, among them is one who is moderate in his disbelief, i.e., among them are those who submit to Allah and understand something of this power, though he errs regarding the idols in that he magnifies them by his conduct and tongue.

"Al-khattar" is the one who is foul in treachery. That is because Allah's favours upon His servants are as if they were covenants and bounties, from which arises the obligation to render their thanks and worship to their Bestower. Whoever denies that and rejects it, it is as if he has betrayed and deceived. From betrayal is the saying of 'Amr ibn Ma'd Yakrib al-Zubaydi:

For if you had seen Abu 'Umayr, you would have filled your hands with treachery and betrayal.

Al-Hasan said: al-khattar is al-ghaddar (the treacherous). "Kafur" is a form of intensification (mubalagha).

The saying of the Exalted and Majestic:

However, what God, the Exalted, has kept exclusively to Himself is the knowledge of the time, while other things He has informed some of His servants about part of it. Likewise, the sending down of rain is a matter whose details and the knowledge of its specific time God, the Exalted and Majestic, has kept to Himself. Ibn Abi 'Abla read "bi-ayyati ardin" with a fatha on the ya' and an added feminine ta' (ta' ta'nith). ﴿All-Knowing, All-Aware﴾ are two qualifiers similar in meaning to the sense of the verse.

Ibn Mas'ud, may God be pleased with him, said: "Your Prophet was given everything except the keys of the five," and then he recited the verse.

(p-٦٤) "Wa yunzilu al-ghayth" with a light (unstressed) pronunciation was read by the people of Kufa, Abu 'Amr and 'Isa. "Yunazzilu" with the emphatic (tathqil) form was read by Nafi', Abu Ja'far, 'Asim and Shayba. Abu Hatim mentioned an opinion favouring the emphatic form.

Likewise, the sending down of rain is a matter whose details and the knowledge of its specific time God, the Exalted and Majestic, has kept to Himself. The matter of embryos is likewise, and the actions of people and all their earnings are likewise, and the place where every human dies is likewise, as are the regions and the specific location of the body.

Ibn Abi 'Abla read "bi-ayyati ardin" with a fatha on the ya' and an added feminine ta' (ta' ta'nith). ﴿All-Knowing, All-Aware﴾ are two qualifiers similar in meaning to the sense of the verse.

Ibn Mas'ud, may God be pleased with him, said: "Your Prophet was given everything except the keys of the five," and then he recited the verse.

(p-٦٤) "Wa yunzilu al-ghayth" with a light (unstressed) pronunciation was read by the people of Kufa, Abu 'Amr and 'Isa. "Yunazzilu" with the emphatic (tathqil) form was read by Nafi', Abu Ja'far, 'Asim and Shayba. Abu Hatim mentioned an opinion favouring the emphatic form.

The commentary of Surat Luqman is complete, and praise is to God, Lord of the worlds.

And may God bless our master Muhammad, and his family and companions, and grant them peace.
